annotations.description: Haiku Coach declined to cast Fatal Push on Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer during their own precombat main phase. Ragavan is a high-value threat that generates card advantage and Treasure tokens every time it connects. Fatal Push can destroy it (mana value 1, well within the 2-or-less threshold). While waiting until the opponent's combat to cast it is sometimes correct, there's no downside to killing Ragavan now since it's already on the battlefield and the opponent has tapped-out lands. Additionally, Haiku Coach has Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth making all lands Swamps, so they have plenty of black mana available. The 'reasoning' suggests they thought it was the opponent's turn, but it's actually Haiku Coach's own precombat main - this appears to be a misread of the game state. However, Ragavan could also be attacked into with Nethergoyf, so killing it with Push while it could be dealt with in combat is a minor resource waste. The real issue is passing without doing anything when they could have removed a dangerous threat.

annotations.description: Casting Phlage for its normal mana cost (1RW) means it will immediately be sacrificed upon entering the battlefield because it didn't escape. This wastes the card entirely - Phlage's ETB trigger will deal 3 damage and gain 3 life, but then it's sacrificed. The player has 7 cards in graveyard and needs to exile 5 + pay RRWW for escape. With Leyline of the Guildpact making all lands every basic type, they have access to all colors. They should have used the Escape option instead, which keeps Phlage on the battlefield as a 6/6. Looking at the choices, there ARE two 'Cast Phlage with Escape' options available. The player has enough cards in graveyard (7 cards) and with Leyline of the Guildpact, their lands produce any color, so they can pay RRWW from their 5 available lands (Steam Vents, Mountain, Indatha Triome, Wooded Foothills if cracked, plus one more). Actually, Wooded Foothills is untapped but would need to be sacrificed first. Let's count untapped lands: Steam Vents, Mountain, Indatha Triome, Wooded Foothills = 4 lands. RRWW costs 4 mana. They could crack Wooded Foothills (paying 1 life, going to 7) to get a land, giving them 5 lands total but only 4 untapped non-Foothills lands. Actually Wooded Foothills produces mana via sacrifice, so they'd have: the fetched land + Steam Vents + Mountain + Indatha Triome = 4 mana sources. RRWW = 4 mana. This works! They should escape Phlage instead of hard-casting it to waste it.

annotations.betterLine: Cast Phlage via Escape ({R}{R}{W}{W}, exile 5 cards from graveyard) to keep it on the battlefield as a 6/6 with the ETB trigger of 3 damage and 3 life. Crack Wooded Foothills first for a land, then use 4 lands to pay RRWW and exile 5 of the 7 graveyard cards.

Even if the intent was to kill it after it resolves, Phlage is a 6/6 which exceeds Fatal Push's mana value limit (MV 3), making it an illegal target. Additionally, Phlage will sacrifice itself upon entering since it wasn't escaped (cast from graveyard with escape cost). annotations.description: Opponent cast Thoughtseize, which is a noncreature spell on the stack. Gem3F Johnny had Stubborn Denial in hand and the mana/ability to cast it (Steam Vents can produce U, though it's tapped — but Wooded Foothills is untapped and with Leyline of the Guildpact all lands are every basic type, so fetching could produce U). Actually, looking more carefully: Steam Vents, Mountain, and Indatha Triome are all tapped. Wooded Foothills is untapped but needs to be sacrificed to fetch. With Leyline of the Guildpact, Wooded Foothills is every basic land type and can tap for any color including U. So they could tap Wooded Foothills for U and cast Stubborn Denial to counter Thoughtseize. Even without Ferocious, Stubborn Denial would counter unless opponent pays {1}, and opponent has no untapped lands (Swamp, Ifnir Deadlands x2, Urborg are their lands — need to check). Looking at opponent's board: Swamp, Ifnir Deadlands, Construct Token, Ifnir Deadlands, Nethergoyf, Urborg. The opponent likely tapped lands to cast Thoughtseize (costs {B}, so one land tapped). With Urborg making all lands Swamps, opponent could have multiple untapped lands to pay {1}. However, Stubborn Denial without Ferocious is still worth trying — it forces opponent to have and spend an extra mana. But more importantly, Gem3F Johnny declined to counter and let Thoughtseize resolve, revealing their hand. With only 3 cards in hand (Stubborn Denial, Territorial Kavu, Leyline of the Guildpact), losing any of these is significant. Actually wait — with Leyline of the Guildpact making all nonland permanents all colors, and Territorial Kavu being a creature, Kavu's power equals 5 (all basic land types). That means Ferocious would be active if Kavu were on the battlefield, but it's in hand. No Ferocious. Without Ferocious, opponent can pay {1} to avoid the counter. Opponent likely has untapped lands to pay {1}. So Stubborn Denial might not actually counter it. Still, making them pay {1} has some value, and there's a chance they're tapped out. Let me reconsider — Thoughtseize costs {B}. Opponent has Swamp, 2x Ifnir Deadlands, Urborg. With Urborg, all lands tap for B. So they tapped one land for Thoughtseize and likely have 2-3 untapped lands. They can easily pay {1}. So declining Stubborn Denial is actually reasonable since it wouldn't counter the spell. But wait — even using Stubborn Denial means it goes to graveyard and isn't revealed/lost to Thoughtseize. If they use it now (even if countered by paying {1}), they protect Territorial Kavu from being taken by Thoughtseize since the opponent would only see Kavu and Leyline. Actually no, if Stubborn Denial resolves (fails to counter), it goes to graveyard, and then Thoughtseize resolves revealing only Kavu and Leyline. That's actually a consideration — using Stubborn Denial to 'protect' the more important card. But opponent can still take Kavu. Hmm, this is more nuanced than initially apparent.
annotations.actionTaken: Declined to cast Stubborn Denial in response to Thoughtseize, allowing it to resolve and reveal full hand.
annotations.betterLine: Cast Stubborn Denial targeting Thoughtseize. Even though opponent likely has mana to pay {1} (no Ferocious), casting it removes Stubborn Denial from hand before Thoughtseize resolves, meaning opponent only sees Territorial Kavu and Leyline of the Guildpact — potentially protecting a more valuable card from being discarded. Additionally, Wooded Foothills with Leyline could tap for U, and sacrificing it would enable Revolt for future plays while the Stubborn Denial going to graveyard adds an instant type for potential Nethergoyf/escape considerations.

However, in this case Gem3F Johnny has no other creatures on board, so Ragavan won't attack this turn regardless (it doesn't have haste unless cast with Dash or given haste by Arena of Glory). That said, Arena of Glory could give haste if used with its exert ability - paying {R}, {T}, exert to add {R}{R}, and if that mana is spent on a creature spell it gains haste. Gem3F Johnny could have cast Ragavan using Arena of Glory's exert ability to give it haste, allowing it to attack this turn and potentially connect for a Treasure token and card exile. Instead, they appear to be casting it with regular mana, missing the haste opportunity. Actually, looking more carefully, the choice is just 'Ragavan' - we don't know which land they tapped. But casting Ragavan in precombat main is correct if they want to attack with it - they'd need haste though. The key question is whether they used Arena of Glory's exert to give haste. annotations.description: At 6 life facing a Nethergoyf and two Eldrazi Spawn tokens, Gem3F Johnny chose to hard-cast Ragavan for {R} instead of using Dash for {1}{R}. Dash gives haste, allowing Ragavan to attack immediately and potentially generate a Treasure token and card advantage. Hard-casting means Ragavan won't attack until next turn, and at 6 life against a board that dealt 6 damage last attack, surviving to next turn is not guaranteed. With Dash, if Ragavan is removed, it would return to hand instead of dying. However, hard-casting does leave Ragavan as a permanent blocker, which could be relevant at 6 life - Ragavan could chump-block the Nethergoyf next turn to survive. The trade-off between having a blocker (hard cast) vs. getting immediate attack value and protection from removal (dash) is debatable, but at 6 life with the opponent having a large Nethergoyf, the blocking argument has merit. Still, Dash would give haste for immediate combat damage, potential Treasure + exile, and if opponent has removal Ragavan returns to hand safely.
